newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Metals - China "lump sum" package cuts duties.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - China "lump sum" package cuts duties.

text.p: Importers of metal into China can cut their costs by accepting a so-called lump-sum package organised by local trading firms to help avoid high import-related taxes, trade sources said on Monday.
"Of course, it is cheaper than the regular channels, saving them (importers) money and it is more efficient," an aluminium trader at a Chinese firm in Hong Kong said.
He and others said the services are offered at Chinese ports in the south and charges can vary but are invariably cheaper than costs incurred through official import channels.
Import duty and value-added tax (VAT) add 20 percent to the cost of imported copper and 26 percent to the cost of imported aluminium, traders in Shanghai said.
The lump sum charges include the import duty and VAT, plus the cost of unloading and transport to warehouses, a Shanghai trader said.
Western and Chinese traders have said a hefty proportion of both copper and aluminium coming into China does not show up on customs figures because it does not traverse official channels.

While traders have said smuggled material could be as much again as that reported by customs, Beijing's official trading arm, the China Non-Ferrous Metal Import and Export Corp (CNIEC), has said the amounts are quite small.
Traders told Reuters the lump sum charges are just another way of avoiding the high import costs.
Meanwhile, the domestic markets remain quiet as prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) strengthen.

One trader in Shanghai with a major Western firm said Chinese traders have been offering to sell their copper back to the market at the LME cash price, with no premium, in an effort to take advantage of the current levels.
The offers were in small lots, she said, adding, "There is no interest".
The LME saw prices close the afternoon kerb at $2,520 a tonne, down $6 from Thursday's kerb close. A lot of buying interest was seen, although prices ran into some resistance above $2,520.
Profit-taking was seen ahead of the long weekend. The LME is closed on Monday for a bank holiday.

Physical prices in the Shanghai area have cooled in the past week or so, now standing at around 23,100-23,200 yuan ($2,783-$2,795) a tonne on rumours of pending arrivals of 150,000-160,000 tonnes of copper.
Most sources remain sceptical of the rumours, saying they do not expect to see Chinese buying while LME prices remain so high and while the domestic market supply appears adequate.
No change was reported in premium levels.
The Chinese offers at LME cash have kept the premiums, on a cost and freight basis to Hong Kong, in a range between zero and $100 a tonne for cathode.
Aluminium ingots continue to arrive in Hong Kong on a C&F basis carrying a premium of $95 to $110 a tonne, traders said.
Lead and nickel were described as catatonic, and zinc continues to move from China into LME warehouses in Singapore as prices of that metal remain firm.
Zinc closed on the LME at $1,363 on Friday, down $1, after trading in a narrow band.
-- Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544
